title: Hell (CCC 1033–1037)
hookLine: the Church teaches it as self-exclusion from God, and prays that none be lost

cards: Outside the old walls of Jerusalem there's a valley. Its Hebrew name is Ge Hinnom, the valley of Hinnom. In the Bible's darkest chapters it was a place of terrible worship, and the prophets cursed it.
Later, tradition says, it became associated with burning and refuse. When Jesus warned his listeners about the ultimate loss, he used that valley's name.
In Greek it became Gehenna, and English Bibles usually translate it as hell. So the word starts with a real place people could point to.

teach.b: Jesus speaks about hell often in the Gospels, and the Church takes his warnings seriously. The Catechism defines hell as a state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God and the blessed.
Not a trap God springs on people: a final, free refusal of love. Why is it possible at all? The Catechism says no one can be united with God unless they freely choose to love him.
Love can't be forced. If a person can truly say yes, they can truly say no.
The chief pain of hell, the Church says, is being separated from God, the only one in whom a human being can find the life and happiness they were made for. And no one is sent there by design.

teach.h: GOD PREDESTINES NO ONE TO HELL.
teach.b: The Catechism states that God predestines no one to go to hell; it takes a willful turning away, persisted in to the end.
The Gospel's warnings, it says, are a call to responsibility and to conversion, not a threat meant to frighten.

teach.h: THE CHURCH PRAYS NONE BE LOST.
teach.b: So the Church prays that no one be lost, leaning on two verses. First Timothy: God "will have all men to be saved."
And Second Peter: the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance." At every Mass using the Roman Canon, the Church asks to be saved from final damnation.
It has declared many people saints, in heaven. It has never declared any particular person to be in hell.
Catholics hold two things together: the teaching is real, and the Church prays for all.

how: At Mass the Church prays to be saved from final damnation, and many Catholics add the Fatima prayer to each decade of the rosary, asking that all souls be led to heaven, especially those most in need of mercy.

o: a waiting room before everyone goes to heaven
a punishment God picks for people he's angry at
a final, free refusal of God's love

games.q: the Catechism explains why hell is possible at all. what reason does it give?
o: God needs some people to be punished.
we can't be united with God unless we freely choose to love him.
some people are made for it from birth.
games.why: love can't be forced. a real yes means a real no is possible, and hell is that final refusal.

practice: Think of someone who seems lost, or hard, or turned away: someone you know, or someone in the news whose cruelty you can't understand. Don't excuse what they've done; just hold them in mind as a person God made.
If you pray, ask God to have mercy on them and bring them home; if you don't, simply wish them turned toward the good.

wordCard.voice: Hell. In Catholic teaching, the state of definitive self-exclusion from God, a final refusal of love, and the reason the Church prays that no one be lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from Hebrew Ge Hinnom, the valley of Hinnom: the word Jesus uses for hell.

carryVoice: Your line: the church prays for all. Even the ones hardest to pray for. That's three hundred twenty-seven days.
